characters: Yao: a ten-year-old Ghanaian boy in Primary 4, energetic and observant, wearing a bright orange polo shirt and navy shorts.
Akosua: Yao’s nine-year-old classmate and neighbour, neat braided hair with green beads, wearing a green-and-white checked dress.
Mr Mensah: their Primary 4 teacher, wearing a collared cream shirt and carrying a clipboard.
Honourable Tetteh: the local Assembly Member, wearing a neat blue northern smock and carrying an official work schedule.

narrationPlan.voice: Lively, warm Ghanaian storyteller (en-GH); enthusiastic for Yao and Akosua, caring and firm on safety for Mr Mensah, respectful for Honourable Tetteh.
narrationPlan.pace: Medium-slow (about 110 words per minute) for Primary 3–5.

music: Optional cheerful marimba and light shaker rhythm; off by default.
culturalNotes: Highlights the real civic role of the elected Assembly Member in Ghanaian local government.
reviewQuestions: Are the child-safety boundaries (no entering drains, no hazardous waste) and the balance between citizen habits and municipal accountability clear?

pages.brief: Busy Ghanaian neighbourhood street: a bread seller, a driver and a tailor gesturing in frustration toward windblown plastic sachets and a full waste bin in the background, while Yao (10, orange polo shirt, navy shorts) and Akosua (9, green beads, green-and-white dress) observe thoughtfully.
pages.narration: Lively, rhythmic opening capturing the everyday chorus of "Why hasn’t Somebody fixed this yet?".

pages.brief: Bright Ghanaian primary classroom: Akosua raising her hand at her desk while Mr Mensah (cream collared shirt) smiles kindly and holds up a calm open palm to explain safety rules.
pages.narration: Immediate, clear child-safety boundary from Mr Mensah.

pages.brief: Mr Mensah pointing to a two-part classroom illustration on the board: on one side adult municipal workers in high-visibility vests and boots operating a desilting truck; on the other side children sorting clean dry plastic bottles into colour-coded bins (no text).
pages.narration: Crucial distinction: children never do hazardous cleanup or replace public sanitation services, but practice safe waste sorting and civic engagement.

pages.brief: Clean sunny school courtyard: Mr Mensah supervising as Yao, Akosua and classmates wearing clean gardening gloves place dry plastic water bottles into a green barrel and scrap paper into a blue barrel (no text on barrels).
pages.narration: Upbeat, safe, age-appropriate school waste segregation.

pages.brief: By the school gate: a smiling recycling worker in a green vest weighing large net sacks of clean plastic bottles on a hanging scale beside a small pickup van, while Mr Mensah, Yao and Akosua cheer.
pages.narration: Walk through the arithmetic clearly: 40 kg plastic + 20 kg paper = 60 kg; 40 kg × 2 cedis = 80 cedis for library books.

pages.brief: Safe sidewalk view: Mr Mensah and two parents walking beside Yao and Akosua, who stand well back on the dry pavement marking coloured dots on a hand-drawn street map on a clipboard (no text).
pages.narration: Show safe, adult-supervised civic observation and data collection.

pages.brief: School assembly hall meeting: Yao and Akosua standing beside Mr Mensah and parents, showing their colourful street map (with red and green pin icons, no text) to Honourable Tetteh (wearing a blue smock) and an environmental health officer.
pages.narration: Model constructive, respectful engagement between citizens, schools and local government.

pages.brief: Close view at the meeting table: Honourable Tetteh placing green checkmarks on the street map while shopkeepers, parents and Mr Mensah applaud.
pages.narration: Explain clearly why local government is accountable: citizens pay tolls and rates, and the Assembly provides scheduled public services.

pages.brief: Sunny Saturday morning on Market Street: adult municipal sanitation workers in high-visibility vests, gloves and tall boots clearing the roadside drain into a dump truck, while adult shopkeepers sweep their dry verandas and place lidded bins by their stalls; Yao and Akosua watch happily from the school veranda with Mr Mensah.
pages.narration: Show the proper division of labour: adult crews handle heavy drains and trucks, adult traders maintain covered bins, and children stay safe.

pages.brief: Clean, vibrant Ghanaian street after a light rain: clear drains, neat lidded bins along the pavement, smiling shopkeepers, and Yao, Akosua, Mr Mensah and Honourable Tetteh giving a thumbs-up.

teacherGuide.overview: A Primary 3–5 citizenship and environmental health story that teaches learners how to move from passive complaining to safe, constructive action. It enforces strict child-safety rules (children never enter drains or touch hazardous waste), teaches waste segregation and numeracy (40 kg + 20 kg = 60 kg; 40 × 2 = 80 cedis), and shows how citizens partner with their Assembly Member and District Assembly Environmental Health Department.
learningGoals: Explain why children must never enter roadside drains or handle sharp/hazardous waste, and identify safe environmental actions (sorting clean dry plastic/paper, using bins).
Calculate total recycled weight (40 kg + 20 kg = 60 kg) and recycling income (40 kg × 2 cedis = 80 cedis).
Describe the role of the Assembly Member and the District Assembly Environmental Health / Waste Management Department.
Explain why clean communities require both responsible personal habits and accountable public services.

beforeReading: Preview the title and cover illustration with learners and ask what real-world problem or question the characters might face.
whileReading: Pause at the embedded comprehension and vocabulary activities to check understanding and discuss the evidence in the text.
afterReading: Three-Barrel Classroom Sort: Label three boxes "Clean Plastic", "Clean Paper/Card", and "Organic Peels (Compost)". Call out 10 everyday school items and have pupils point to the correct box (plus a 4th "Adult Hazard Report Only" card for broken glass or batteries).
Letter to Our Assembly Member: Draft a polite, factual class letter thanking local sanitation workers and suggesting one specific improvement (such as a lidded bin near the school gate).
discussion: Why did everyone on Market Street keep asking "Why hasn’t Somebody fixed this yet?" while nobody took the first step?
Why did Mr Mensah praise Akosua’s caring heart but firmly forbid the class from climbing into the roadside gutter?
How did bringing a neat map and 60 signatures to Honourable Tetteh work better than shouting complaints on the street?
Why shouldn’t children ever be expected to replace the District Assembly’s adult sanitation workers?
reflection: Why shouldn’t children ever be expected to replace the District Assembly’s adult sanitation workers?

whatWeKnow: Separating clean dry plastics and paper at source prevents contamination and makes recycling economically viable, while keeping solid waste out of storm drains prevents urban flash flooding and mosquito breeding.
In Ghana, Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies (MMDAs) are statutorily responsible for waste management and public environmental health.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Ghanaian materials engineers are testing ways to blend shredded waste plastic with sand to mould durable pavement blocks and kerbstones.

investigation.title: Clean Dry Classroom Waste Tally (No Touching Litter!)
materials: A notebook, pencil, and your own school bag or desk after break time.
steps: Without touching any ground litter, look at the clean wrappers or scrap paper from your own snack and exercise book today.
Classify each item into one of three columns in your notebook: Column 1 (Paper/Card), Column 2 (Clean Plastic), Column 3 (Fruit Peel/Organic).
Add the class totals on the chalkboard to see how many items a single classroom can keep out of the bin every week by sorting and using reusable water bottles!
